# Retroperitoneal hematoma

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General trauma > Retroperitoneal hematoma*

[Original Article Link](/library/ov00aR)

---

## Summary

<u>Retroperitoneal</u> <u>hematoma</u> (RPH) is bleeding into the <u>retroperitoneal space</u>, which may occur spontaneously (most often in patients on <u>anticoagulants</u>), after blunt or <u>penetrating trauma</u>, or <u>iatrogenically</u> following procedures such as <u>percutaneous coronary intervention</u>. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with flank, back, abdominal, and/or leg <u>pain</u>. Significant bleeding can lead to <u>hemodynamic instability</u>. CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast is the diagnostic modality of choice and may demonstrate contrast extravasation if there is ongoing bleeding. Most spontaneous and <u>iatrogenic</u> RPHs can be <u>managed conservatively</u> with close observation, <u>transfusions</u>, and correction of coagulopathies (e.g., <u>anticoagulant reversal</u>). <u>Angiographic embolization</u> or <u>surgery</u> may be necessary if bleeding persists despite <u>conservative treatment</u>. Complications include <u>hemorrhagic shock</u> and <u>abdominal compartment syndrome</u>.

---

## Etiology

* Traumatic RPH [[2]](/library/ZyYZd7)[[6]](/library/BzXzE00)

* <u>Blunt abdominopelvic trauma</u>

* <u>Penetrating abdominopelvic trauma</u>

* Spontaneous RPH [[7]](/library/fHdkpr0)[[8]](/library/2HdTpr0)

* <u>Malignancy</u> (e.g., renal or <u>adrenal</u> tumors)

* Hereditary or acquired coagulopathies (e.g., antiplatelet or <u>anticoagulant</u> use)

* Leaking or <u>ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm</u>

* <u>Postpartum retroperitoneal hematoma</u> (e.g., after <u>uterine rupture</u>)

* <u>Iatrogenic</u> RPH [[4]](/library/YAWnRL0)[[5]](/library/7td4U70)

* Endovascular procedures (e.g., <u>cardiac catheterization</u>)

* Surgical interventions (e.g., <u>nephrectomy</u>, <u>retroperitoneal</u> dissection)

* <u>Postpartum retroperitoneal hematoma</u> (e.g., <u>uterine artery</u> injury during <u>Cesarean delivery</u>)

---

## Clinical features

Clinical features vary based on <u>hematoma</u> size, bleeding rate, and <u>mass effect</u> on nearby organs. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with nonspecific symptoms. [[7]](/library/fHdkpr0)[[9]](/library/SHdypr0)




* Abdominal, flank, and/or <u>back pain</u>

* Hip and/or leg <u>pain</u>

* Inguinal swelling and/or tenderness

* <u>Ecchymosis</u> (e.g., <u>Grey Turner sign</u>, <u>Cullen sign</u>) [[10]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Femoral neuropathy</u>  [[11]](/library/Eyd8Ss0)

* <u>Clinical features of shock</u> (e.g., <u>hemodynamic instability</u>)

---

## Diagnosis

For suspected traumatic RPH, see also “<u>Urgent diagnostics for trauma patients</u>.”




### Approach




* Consider RPH in patients with abdominal, flank, and/or <u>back pain</u> and who have <u>signs of shock</u>.

* Obtain CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast.

* Obtain initial <u>laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>coagulation studies</u>, <u>type and screen</u>).





### Imaging [[12]](/library/JydsTs0)




* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast (recommended) [[6]](/library/BzXzE00)[[7]](/library/fHdkpr0)

* To determine size and location of <u>hematoma</u>

* To evaluate for recent and/or active bleeding

* <u>MRI</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> [[7]](/library/fHdkpr0)

* Comparable diagnostic <u>accuracy</u> to CT

* Limited by availability and study duration

* <u>Ultrasound</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> (not recommended) [[12]](/library/JydsTs0)

* Cannot evaluate the entire <u>retroperitoneum</u>

* Cannot detect active bleeding

* May miss small RPHs





> [!WARNING]
> <u>FAST</u> has limited <u>sensitivity</u> for RPH and should not be used in isolation when RPH is suspected. [[13]](/library/RtblWv)

---

## Management

Management depends on etiology and hemodynamic stability of the patient, with guidance largely based on expert consensus. A multidisciplinary approach (e.g., <u>surgery</u>, interventional radiology) is often required.




### Approach [[3]](/library/THd6pr0)[[7]](/library/fHdkpr0)[[14]](/library/Bydzhs0)




* Stabilize <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients using the <u>ABCDE approach</u>.

* Initiate <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u>.

* Transfuse <u>blood products</u> as needed for <u>hemorrhagic shock</u>.

* <u>Correct coagulopathy</u> and consider <u>anticoagulant reversal</u>.

* Traumatic RPH

* Begin <u>interventions for pelvic hemorrhage control</u> as needed.

* Evaluate for indications for <u>emergency exploratory laparotomy</u>.

* Consult <u>surgery</u> and interventional radiology to evaluate need for surgical and/or interventional management.

* Admit patient for <u>hemodynamic monitoring</u>, <u>serial hemoglobin and hematocrit</u>, and repeat imaging.





### <u>Conservative management</u> [[3]](/library/THd6pr0)[[14]](/library/Bydzhs0)[[15]](/library/LtdwV70)




* Indications

* Nontraumatic RPH: hemodynamically stable patients without active contrast extravasation on CT

* Traumatic RPH: <u>blunt abdominopelvic trauma</u> without other indications for <u>exploratory laparotomy</u>

* General measures

* Monitor for changes in clinical status (e.g., <u>vital signs</u>, <u>serial abdominal examinations</u>).

* Serial <u>laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>hemoglobin</u>)

* Repeat imaging for RPH expansion





### Surgical and interventional management [[3]](/library/THd6pr0)[[7]](/library/fHdkpr0)[[14]](/library/Bydzhs0)




* Indications

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u> not responsive to resuscitation

* Ongoing bleeding despite <u>anticoagulant reversal</u>

* <u>Penetrating trauma</u> with associated organ or vascular injury

* Expanding RPH on repeat imaging

* Compressive symptoms (e.g., <u>femoral neuropathy</u>)

* Interventions

* <u>Angiographic embolization</u> (e.g., <u>endovascular coiling</u>)

* Open surgical exploration and <u>hemorrhage control</u>  [[16]](/library/xd1EHf0)
